source.title: The Effect of Combined Strength Training on Vertical Jump Performance in Young Basketball Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

paper.citation: Uysal, H. Ş., Dalkiran, O., Korkmaz, S., Akyildiz, Z., Nobari, H., & Clemente, F. M. (2023). The effect of combined strength training on vertical jump performance in young basketball players: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Strength & Conditioning Journal, 45(5), 554–567. https://doi.org/10.1519/SSC.0000000000000762
paper.abstract: Compared with traditional strength training or basketball-only training, what is the effect of combined strength training on vertical-jump performance in competitive basketball players younger than 25, and do jump type, age, program duration, comparator, or combined-training format modify the effect? Eleven controlled studies of competitive basketball players younger than 25 were included; 82% of participants were male and only one study was exclusively female. The authors report 833 participants, with 433 in combined training and 399 in comparator groups; those subgroup counts sum to 832, an internal numerical discrepancy. Interventions paired high-intensity strength exercises with lower-intensity plyometric or sport-specific exercises in complex, contrast, or other combined formats. PRISMA-guided systematic review registered prospectively in PROSPERO (CRD42022306065), searching Google Scholar, PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect and updating the search in September 2022. Two reviewers extracted data, a third checked disagreements, and included studies were assessed with TESTEX; studies scoring 4 or less were excluded. Random-effects standardized mean differences were pooled; I², funnel-plot methods, Egger’s test, fail-safe N, sensitivity analysis, subgroups, and meta-regression were used.
paper.tldr: This review evaluates chronic programs combining higher-intensity resistance and lower-intensity plyometric exercises for vertical-jump development in young basketball players and identifies substantial uncertainty behind protocol-specific recommendations. The initial pooled effect favored combined strength training (SMD=1.11, 95% CI 0.63–1.60), but heterogeneity was high (I²=82%). Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review registered prospectively in PROSPERO (CRD42022306065), searching Google Scholar, PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect and updating the search in September 2022. Two reviewers extracted data, a third checked disagreements, and included studies were assessed with TESTEX; studies scoring 4 or less were excluded. Random-effects standardized mean differences were pooled; I², funnel-plot methods, Egger’s test, fail-safe N, sensitivity analysis, subgroups, and meta-regression were used.
paper.findings: The initial pooled effect favored combined strength training (SMD=1.11, 95% CI 0.63–1.60), but heterogeneity was high (I²=82%). After removing six outcomes labeled extreme values, the pooled effect remained positive but smaller (SMD=0.82, 95% CI 0.58–1.06) and heterogeneity fell to I²=47%. Subgroup analyses reported larger effects for 10-week programs and athletes aged at least 18, but meta-regression did not support training duration as a predictor; only age was statistically associated with effect size (R²=22%). No statistically significant difference was found among complex, contrast, and other combined-training formats. Certainty was rated moderate because of indirectness and imprecision.
paper.limitations: Search and inclusion were limited to English-language reports, and only a small number of studies informed each moderator. Most participants were male, no included players were older than 25, and female-specific inference is unsupported. The paper contains internal reporting inconsistencies: included-study accounting is unclear, participant subgroup counts do not equal the stated total, the methods print p<0.5 as the significance threshold, and the conclusion’s age wording conflicts with the subgroup result. Twenty-eight test outcomes were pooled from 11 studies, but the reported analysis does not clearly describe adjustment for correlated outcomes within studies; treating them as independent could overstate precision. High initial heterogeneity and post hoc removal of extreme outcomes make the magnitude sensitive to analytic decisions. Funnel-plot and Egger tests have low power with few studies, so “no publication bias” is not proof that bias is absent. Jump height is a performance surrogate; the review does not establish effects on basketball performance, injury, durability, or collegiate American-football transfer.
paper.practicalImplications: Combined resistance-plus-plyometric programming is a plausible option for improving vertical jump in young basketball players, but the exact effect size and optimal duration or format are uncertain. Do not adopt the review’s exact two-days-per-week or 10-week prescription as a universal rule. Select exercises, sequence, dose, and recovery from athlete training age, technical competence, sport demands, and existing load, then track jump and strength response locally. Transfer to collegiate American football should be treated as indirect.

paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
